content:
Code discovered in the camera app of the latest iOS 27 beta appears to hint at several major professional photography and videography features on the way.

While the built-in camera app has been steadily gaining features, this discovery is genuinely surprising for an app whose primary purpose is snapshots…

Apple has always tried to strike a balance between making its own camera app extremely easy to use for snapshots, while still giving creative control to those who like to treat it as a professional camera. But despite the app gradually evolving, most keen photographers and videographers still tend to use third-party apps.

If these findings are true, the camera app is about to gain some powerful features usually only found on professional cameras, and the situation may well change. Developer pdfu says he has found code supporting four major features that are not yet enabled in the current beta.

Exposure Aids

Judging exposure by eye is actually very unreliable, especially when trying to view the iPhone screen in harsh sunlight. Most professional cameras offer a histogram, which gives the user an accurate readout of exposure, while video editing software typically uses a waveform to display the same kind of information. Pdfu says he has found code for both of these in the beta.

Focus Peaking

How much of a photo, from the closest foreground to the farthest background, falls within the zone of focus depends on a number of factors, and in some cases only part of the scene will be sharp. Again, judging by eye which areas are in focus and which are not is not very reliable, which is why professional cameras in particular use a method called focus peaking.

When this feature is turned on, an overlay appears on the screen that highlights the parts of the photo that are in focus, usually in red — although the example on the left uses yellow.

Blown Highlights Warning

The worst consequence of an exposure mistake is overexposure. Generally speaking, if you underexpose the shadows, you can usually rescue them in post-processing — unless you get it really wrong, in which case the shadows go completely black (RGB value of zero). Overexposure is far more troublesome, because it is very easy to completely clip the highlights, meaning the bright areas exceed an RGB value of 255 and cannot be recovered.

Many professional cameras offer a feature called zebra indicators, which marks completely overexposed areas with red stripes. In some cases, you can set this threshold manually, for example at 90%, so you get a warning as you approach overexposure rather than only discovering it once it has happened.

This feature is also shown in the image on the right above.

Manual Focus

The current camera app lets you lock the focus to a point in the scene, but it has to be done alongside AE/AF lock, which locks the exposure to the same point.

The report says Apple has been testing a true manual focus feature in the camera app, operated by a slider. Pdfu says this feature may be limited to one or more upcoming new iPhones.

Other Features

In addition to the professional-grade features, an option is reportedly on the way to let you take a burst of timed self-portraits. When taking group photos, a lot of people want to take more than one shot, so this feature would let you set the iPhone on a tripod or somewhere else, take a burst of photos, and then pick one that everyone is happy with.

Finally, there are signs that a new image processing pipeline will be adopted to accommodate the variable aperture expected to appear on the iPhone 18 Pro.

9to5Mac's Take

None of the features above are enabled in the current iOS 27 beta, and I would be surprised if Apple actually put these in the built-in camera app rather than restricting them to Final Cut Camera, but it does look plausible.
